titulo: Ask the question whose answer fits in your head
subtitulo: C'è asks whether the thing exists — and yes or no is an answer you can actually carry
cena: A stranger is drawing your route in the air with both hands, three streets deep, and you lost it at the second turn.
frasePiso: The best direction question is the one that gives you a usable next move, not the most complete answer.

clique.desconto: Nobody handed you four direction questions. You built the ladder yourself out of one opening, by deciding each time how much answer you actually needed.
clique.piso: Next time someone starts drawing a route in the air, you will not try to hold the whole paragraph. You will cut it to a decision before it gets away.

steps.pt: Ask where something is and you get three streets and a hand wave. Start smaller — ask whether it exists at all.
The frame is c'è, plus the thing. The answer is yes or no, and yes or no fits in your head.
Is there a pharmacy near here?

steps.promptPt: You need medicine but do not know if this street has a pharmacy. Ask the yes-or-no question first. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is there a pharmacy near here?
Yes, at the end of the street.
The opening holds; the thing changes. You want any cash machine, not a particular one.

steps.promptPt: You need cash. Keep the frame, swap the thing. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is there a cash machine near here?
Bancomat is the word — it is what the machine is called, and asking for an ATM will slow you down.

steps.promptPt: Simplest possible existence question, in a café. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is there wifi?

steps.es: Sì, la password è sul tavolo.
steps.pt: Yes, the password is on the table.
steps.tts: Sì, la password è sul tavolo.

steps.pt: Now the answer that is too large. Do not ask for the same paragraph again — collapse it into distance.

steps.es: Allora, prende la seconda a destra, poi sempre dritto fino alla chiesa, e dopo la piazza gira a sinistra.
steps.pt: So, take the second right, then straight on to the church, and after the square turn left.
steps.tts: Allora, prende la seconda a destra, poi sempre dritto fino alla chiesa, e dopo la piazza gira a sinistra.
steps.acao: Do not try to hold it. Ask è lontano? instead.

steps.promptPt: You lost the middle. Ask only whether it is far. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is it far?
No, ten minutes on foot.

steps.promptPt: Ten minutes still leaves the first turn unclear. Move it to the map. Speak now.
steps.pt: Can you show me on the map?

steps.promptPt: Same frame, completely different scene: a busy restaurant. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is there a free table?

steps.promptPt: You missed the connection. Ask whether another exists. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is there another train?

steps.promptPt: They walked you through it patiently. Thank them. Speak now.
steps.pt: Thank you, very kind of you.

steps.es: C'è una farmacia qui vicino? È lontano? Mi può mostrare sulla mappa?
steps.pinyin: cheh OO-na far-ma-CHEE-a kwee vee-CHEE-no. eh lon-TA-no. mee pwoh mos-TRA-re SUL-la MAP-pa
steps.pt: Shadow the ladder: exists, distance, map.
steps.tts: C'è una farmacia qui vicino? È lontano? Mi può mostrare sulla mappa?

steps.pt: B08 done. C'è asks whether it exists, è lontano? shrinks a paragraph, and the map takes over when words stop moving your feet.

secoes.corpo: Use it whenever yes or no is already valuable. Keep the opening and replace the object — the frame never changes shape.

secoes.titulo: Ci sono is the plural, and you barely need it
secoes.corpo: C'è for one thing, ci sono for several. In practice almost every travel question is singular — c'è un bagno, c'è un treno — so learn the singular properly and let the plural arrive by ear.
The cash machine is il bancomat, and the same word covers the debit card. Asking for an ATM in Italy usually works, but bancomat gets you an answer without the pause.
Destra, sinistra, sempre dritto, in fondo, dopo la piazza — you need to recognise them, not produce them. Your production job is to shrink the answer with è lontano? or move it to the map.

permissao: You are allowed to cut a stranger's answer short. Asking è lontano? or pulling out the map before someone finishes a three-street explanation is not impatience — it is the fastest way to end up somewhere useful instead of nodding through directions you were never going to retain.
espelho: Anyone who has asked for directions at home and lost the thread after 'turn left at the second light' has already lived this exact failure. The instinct to keep nodding rather than interrupt a helpful stranger is universal, not a gap in your Italian.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You ask a simple question and get a long, generous answer with hand gestures, landmarks and a story about the church.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I should have understood all of that, and asking again would be rude.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Italian direction-giving tends to be generous and narrative rather than terse. The length is hospitality, not obstruction — but it produces more than a first-time visitor can hold in one pass.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Reduce rather than repeat: ask è lontano? for a walk-or-not decision, or open the map and ask them to point.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You leave with one usable fact instead of a paragraph you cannot reconstruct two turns later, and the person still gets to be helpful.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not when someone has already reduced it for you — if the answer was è qui, a due passi, a follow-up question asks for detail that was never missing.
